article.title: A Brief Note on Marx: Capital as a Social Relation
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Douglas Dollinger Marx argues this case in his discussion of colonization (Chapter 33, Kapital, Volume 1). According to Marx, Wakefield, a prominent 19th-century writer on colonization, had discovered that capital is not just a thing but a social relation. Wakefield stumbles upon this revelation by accident. It is not a theme that features prominently in the political economy of Marx’s time or ours. It is, however, a central theme in Kapital and is pivotal to his notion of human emancipation. I want to explain what Marx means by this in simple terms. Students of Marx might find this note a bit too basic for Socialism 101, so maybe it is best to see it as a contribution to Socialism 100. Suppose you are a capitalist and that you show up with your capital – machines, factories, patents, etc. – in a land called Manuland. A bit about Manuland. In Manuland income earners work for themselves either in small manufactories or on small farms. A small manufactory is a one-person or several-person shop of some kind, a shoe shop, say. The people in the shop make the shoes, hence the “manufactory”. Let assume, too, that they own the means of production. We have here a small, self-sufficient college of cobblers. Suppose similar colleges of clothiers. Etc. Now assume the farmers in Manuland are one-family farms and that they own their own means of production. Let us finally assume that the cobblers and farmers are all getting by; sure, there are some bad years but, barring bad accident or ill health, they all get by. Both can afford to exchange a bit of their produce, should they enjoy a surplus, but neither can amass the surplus that drives capital accumulation. You show up now as a proud and ambitious capitalist in Manuland, but just before putting the shovel to the ground to build an industrial facility of scale, you discover something troubling: Manuland has no proletariat. Capital therefore has no place in Manuland. Why? Workers in Manuland do not have to depend on the capitalist for work; they have their own work and their own means of production. The political economy of capitalism, unlike the political economy of Manuland, necessitates a class of dependents; the dependency of this class moreover is a direct function of its having no ownership over the means of production. It is the limited privilege of ownership, and specifically ownership of the means of production, that separates the dependency class from the capitalist. Manuland has no capitalist conception of private property; capital as yet has no social significance in Manuland. In other words, capitalism cannot work if the laborerlabourer is free of capitalist dependency. The point deserving emphasis here is that capital itself is a social relation in the simple sense that it establishes a relation of dependency between those who own and those who do not. Those who do not own must work for those who do; given the reality of surplus value (Mehrwert) – workers create much more value than they get paid for – it is virtually guaranteed that their level of pay will not free them from the dependency. Nor of course is it designed to. On the contrary. Capitalism produces a proletariat of necessity; and dependency becomes a permanent feature of capitalist society. Most of us are aware of this dependency; we live it day by day; economists of a capitalistic bent, however, seldom mention it. If it registers at all in the thinking of these economists, it tends to be seen as simply rooted in the nature of human society itself. Capitalism requires that private property in the means of production be restricted to the few; workers by contrast are expected to sacrifice any claim to owning the means of production, an outcome that perpetuates the condition of dependency that constitutes and defines the proletariat. Understanding this notion of dependency opens the door to Marx’s conception of emancipation. Marx was of course keenly aware of the fundamental antagonism between capitalist dependency and the reality of human emancipation. How is it exactly that we can regard people as free who are in fact dependent for survival on a privileged few? Note, again, this few cannot become the many. A world of capitalists is a world without workers. Someone has to do the work, and it is best that this individual be compelled to do it; a free individual may opt not to do it. For capitalism to work, then, a large majority of people must be placed in a condition of dependency and kept there. Abe Lincoln called it wage slavery. Note here that unions can modify the conditions of such dependency and render them less onerous for workers, but they cannot eliminate the basic social relation of dependency that characterizes capitalism. This will require an organized political effort to overcome the exclusive privileges of ownership of private property in the means of production. Human emancipation in its fullest sense awaits the completion of this task. The post A Brief Note on Marx: Capital as a Social Relation first appeared on Rochester Red Star .
